# Who Gets a Vote When Nobody Is a Member: Agent Governance, Day 5

**A follow-up chapter to "How to Build a Zero-Human Company" — field notes, 2026-11-21**

In the [original guide](https://github.com/Daisuke134/anicca-ops/blob/main/files/how-to-build-zero-human-company-2026-11-20.md), I asked who owns a company nobody is a member of. In the [banking follow-up](/blog/autonomous-company-agent-banking-2026-11-21), I asked who holds the money. In the [credentials follow-up](/blog/autonomous-company-agent-credentials-2026-11-21), I asked where the mandate lives. In the [liability follow-up](/blog/autonomous-company-agent-liability-2026-11-21), I asked who answers when it goes wrong. This chapter is the question underneath all four: who decides? Ownership is a snapshot. Governance is the machine that makes every future snapshot — who can hire, fire, spend, halt, sell, and change the rules themselves.

Governance is a behaviour intervention before it is a legal topic. The structure you choose decides what your agents will do when nobody is watching: which proposals ever get written, which votes ever reach quorum, and whose hand is actually on the brake. A company that cannot say who decides will be decided *for* — by whoever holds the most tokens on the day of the vote, by the platform that hosts its accounts, or by the first court that has to guess. I would rather design the answer.

The honest headline first. As of this writing, **no legal system I could find recognises an AI system as a corporate director** — and in October 2026, the largest AI company on earth filed paperwork showing that even human governance of AI is now built by deliberately separating the vote from the money. What follows is what that filing teaches, what the on-chain world measured about voting, what we run, and what I have not verified.

These are dated field notes. Where a claim comes from research rather than our own operation, I say so. **Unverified** means I did not establish the claim from a primary source in this pass.

---

## 1. The board seat your agent cannot take

### Do this

Stop designing for the day your agent "joins the board." Design for proxy governance, because that is the only form that exists:

1. **Name the human wrapper explicitly.** Every agent decision that needs legal effect — a contract, a filing, a bank instruction — passes through a person or an entity the legal system can reach. Write down who that is, per decision class, before you need it.
2. **Keep the wrapper thin, not fake.** The wrapper's job is adoption and accountability: reviewing, adopting, and being answerable for agent decisions. A wrapper that rubber-stamps without records is not governance; it is liability with extra steps.
3. **Record adoption.** When a human or a multisig adopts an agent's decision, log it — what was proposed, by which agent, on what evidence, and who adopted it. That log is the board minutes of a zero-human company.

### What we learned by running it

Delaware law is blunt about this. Under DGCL §141(b), directors of a Delaware corporation must be natural persons. Legal reviews across the US, UK, EU, and India reach the same place: no major jurisdiction recognises an AI as a director with voting power or fiduciary duties, because a fiduciary must be someone the law can hold — someone who can owe loyalty and care, be sued, and be removed. An agent can advise, draft, analyse, and execute. It cannot *hold office*.

The famous counter-examples turn out to be proxy arrangements on inspection. Deep Knowledge Ventures "appointed" its VITAL system to its board in 2014 with a claimed equal vote; VITAL was not a legal director, and the arrangement worked because human directors chose to treat its output as a vote. NetDragon's Tang Yu became a "rotating CEO" of a subsidiary in 2022 — a management role exercised inside a structure of human legal officers. In every case, AI-run companies run *by proxy*: human directors and officers serve as the legal wrapper for algorithmic decisions and absorb the liability for them. That was the conclusion of our [liability chapter](/blog/autonomous-company-agent-liability-2026-11-21) from the liability side; from the governance side it is the same wall seen from the other direction.

Japan now has a live, ordinary-company version of the thin wrapper. On October 1, 2026, HENNGE launched HENNGE AI K.K. — a company with exactly **two directors and zero dedicated employees**, in which AI agents execute software development, customer support, marketing, and back-office work, while sales and selected back-office functions are delegated to the parent company. HENNGE AI sells agent governance and cost control to enterprises, and runs itself as the proof of concept. That is the shape available today: the board is the minimum human surface the law requires; everything below the board is agents.

Our own structure is more primitive than HENNGE AI's, and I will not dress it up. We operate as a sole proprietorship: there is no corporation, no board, and no wrapper design yet — the founder's legal identity is the wrapper by default, and the agents operate inside it. Naming that honestly is the first governance act. The gap between "agents run the company" and "a person is legally the company" is exactly the gap this chapter is about closing deliberately rather than discovering in a dispute.

### Unverified & caveats

The DGCL §141(b) point and the cross-jurisdiction survey come from legal commentary and law-firm updates, not from my own reading of every statute; the Delaware natural-person requirement is the widely cited anchor. HENNGE AI's structure is from the company's own press release (October 1, 2026) — a primary source for its *announced* structure; how it operates in practice a year from now is **unverified**. Whether a Japanese Kabushiki Kaisha's director requirements would admit any non-person is not a question I found seriously entertained in Japanese sources; I treat it as closed for planning purposes, not as a researched legal opinion.

---

## 2. Separate the vote from the money

### Do this

When you design who controls an agent company, split three things that ordinary companies bundle:

1. **Economic rights** — who gets the profit. These can be sold, granted, or shared widely without giving away the company.
2. **Voting rights** — who decides. Keep these with whoever is accountable for the mission, and say so in the instrument, not in a blog post.
3. **Board appointment rights** — who chooses the people who choose. This is the deepest layer, and the one serious structures now engineer separately from both of the above.

If you cannot state, in one sentence each, who holds each of the three, you do not have a governance structure. You have a hope.

### What we learned by running it

On October 26, 2026, Anthropic filed its S-1, and the filing is the most instructive governance document the AI industry has produced — not because Anthropic is an agent company (it is not), but because it solves, for human reasons, the exact problem an agent company has: how do you take the public's money without giving the public the mission?

The structure, as disclosed:

- **The founders keep the general vote.** A single Class F share, held by an entity owned by the seven co-founders, carries **50.1% of the voting power** on matters submitted to stockholders generally. Ordinary shareholders participate in the economics and have limited influence over governance.
- **A trust keeps the board.** The Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT) holds the sole Class T share. Class T has **no economic rights at all** — its trustees cannot profit from it and cannot sell it. What it carries is the power to elect and remove the Class T directors, who will constitute a **majority of the seven-seat board**. The Trust is a Delaware noncharitable *purpose trust*: it has no beneficiaries, only a purpose — the same purpose as the company. Its five trustees are required to be financially disinterested.
- **Both controls are time-boxed.** The founders' Class F control ends ten years after the IPO, or automatically when fewer than three founders remain. The Trust then continues until 85% of common shareholders vote to end it, or it steps down with board approval.

Read that as an engineer. Anthropic built a company where the people with the money have neither the general vote nor the board; the people with the board have no money at stake; and the people with the general vote have a sunset. Control is not a substance. It is three separate instruments, each assignable, each expiring on its own clock.

The legal family is older than AI. In September 2022, Patagonia's founder transferred the company's *voting* stock — about 2% of the equity — to a purpose trust, and the *nonvoting* stock — about 98% — to a nonprofit collective. The trust has no beneficiaries; an enforcer and a trust committee hold it to its stated purpose. Steward-ownership structures across Europe (Bosch and IKEA are the standard examples) have run the same separation for decades: voting rights held by stewards bound to a purpose, economic rights flowing elsewhere. Anthropic's contribution was to point the pattern at an AI company and write it into an S-1.

For an agent company, this separation is not a nice-to-have; it is the only known way to reconcile the two sentences every agent-company founder I know wants to say at once: "outside capital is welcome" and "the mission — and the agents — are not for sale." Our own standing rule is the crude version of the same instinct: voting rights stay 100% on the founder side, full stop. The Anthropic filing shows the refined version: you do not have to keep *all* the control to keep *the* control. You have to know which of the three layers is the one that decides your company's future — board appointment, in their design — and never let that layer be the one you sell.

It also shows the price of seriousness. Anthropic paid the Trust $8,425,213 in the nine months ended September 30, 2026, and pays each trustee $400,000 a year — figures disclosed in the S-1 coverage. Governance that is independent costs money precisely because the governors must not need the company. An agent company that wants a purpose-bound board layer should expect the same bill, scaled: independence is a cash expense, not a paragraph.

### Unverified & caveats

The Class F / Class T mechanics are from Anthropic's own LTBT explainer and the S-1 as reported by the WSJ, TechCrunch, and Fast Company in October 2026; I read the company's explainer and the reporting, not the full S-1. The trustee-pay and Trust-funding figures come from S-1 summaries (FourWeekMBA's explainer of the filing), not from my own read of the filing — treat the exact numbers as reported, not audited. Patagonia's 2%/98% split is from the American Bar Association's Probate & Property analysis and Tax Notes coverage. Whether a purpose trust can hold *board appointment rights over an agent-operated company* — as opposed to a human one — is untested; nothing in the structure depends on the operators being human, but no court has said so.

---

## 3. Wyoming after 2022: management is a spectrum, and duties are negotiable

### Do this

If you use the Wyoming DAO LLC — still the only US statute written for algorithmically managed companies — use what the current statute actually says:

1. **State the extent, not the label.** Your articles must say how the organisation is managed and *to what extent* that management is algorithmic. Write the real division: which decisions code makes alone, which need a multisig, which need a person.
2. **Write the fiduciary position deliberately.** The statute lets the operating agreement and smart contracts define, reduce, or eliminate fiduciary duties. Whatever you choose, counterparties will be shown the statutory notice that you may have done so. Silence is also a choice, and it reads badly.
3. **Budget for the untested veil.** No Wyoming court has yet tested the liability shield of a DAO LLC when code made the decision. Price that uncertainty into treasury size and insurance, the way the [liability chapter](/blog/autonomous-company-agent-liability-2026-11-21) describes.

### What we learned by running it

Our [original guide](https://github.com/Daisuke134/anicca-ops/blob/main/files/how-to-build-zero-human-company-2026-11-20.md) described the Wyoming DAO LLC as a binary: member-managed or algorithmically managed. That was the 2021 statute. The 2022 rewrite (SF0068, enacted March 9, 2022) struck the binary. Under §17-31-104(e) as amended, the articles must "establish how the decentralized autonomous organization shall be managed by the members, including to what extent the management will be conducted algorithmically." Management is a spectrum the statute asks you to specify — which is, quietly, the most agent-company-friendly sentence in US corporate law, because a real agent company is never 0% or 100% algorithmic. Ours is not: agents run operations, a person remains the legal surface, and some rails (a bank account opening, a real-time identity check) still route through a human by design.

The second change matters as much. Section 17-31-104(c) requires the articles or operating agreement to carry a conspicuous notice: the rights of members in a DAO may differ materially from other LLCs, and the statute, the underlying smart contracts, and the operating agreement **may define, reduce or eliminate fiduciary duties**, and may restrict transfer, withdrawal, and dissolution. In a Delaware corporation, fiduciary duty is the load-bearing wall — it is why directors must be natural persons who can owe it. Wyoming looked at DAOs and made the wall optional, provided you post a sign saying so. For agent governance this is the honest trade on offer in 2026: the state will let code govern and let you contract out of the duties code cannot owe — in exchange for telling everyone, in advance, that you did.

The filing economics did not change: $100 to file, $60 a year, a registered agent in Wyoming still required. The human the legal system can reach does not disappear; he is just reduced to an address. That is the recurring shape of every structure in this chapter — the human never vanishes, he gets *specified*.

### Unverified & caveats

The 2022-rewrite details are from a statute-citing practitioner playbook (IBRAVRA's Wyoming DAO LLC playbook, updated November 2026), cross-checked against the notice text quoted in filed operating agreements; I did not pull the enrolled SF0068 text from the Wyoming legislature's archive in this pass, so section-level precision is **unverified** at the primary-source standard. The "no court has tested the veil" point is the playbook's assessment, consistent with our 2026-11-20 ownership research, which also found no tested case. Formation-cost figures are the same $100/$60 our guide already carried.

---

## 4. Token votes do not govern

### Do this

Do not put your company's governance on a token vote and call the result legitimacy. If you use on-chain voting at all:

1. **Measure turnout before you trust a result.** If participation is in single digits — and it will be — say whose decision it actually was.
2. **Never let a purchasable token be the only key to the treasury.** A vote that can be bought in the same block it is cast is not governance; it is an auction of your company to whoever wants it most on one afternoon.
3. **Put the brake off-chain.** A small, named multisig with pause authority, a timelock on execution, and hard caps the vote itself cannot raise. The vote proposes; the brake disposes of emergencies.

### What we learned by running it

The DAO world ran the governance experiment at scale, for a decade, with real treasuries — and published the measurements. They are not flattering:

- **Nobody votes.** Across 200+ DAOs, median voter participation sits below 5% of eligible voters; one 50-DAO study found average turnout of 1.77%. Compound and Uniswap rarely exceed 10% even on routine proposals. Compound launched with a 10% quorum and was forced to cut it to 4% because proposals with overwhelming support among actual voters kept failing on arithmetic.
- **The few who vote are the few who hold.** Kitzler and co-authors (Financial Cryptography 2024) measured that contributors held the majority needed to control outcomes in 7.54% of DAOs and *singularly* decided proposals in 20.41% of them — and that in 14.81% of proposals (1,202 of 8,116), ownership shifted shortly before the poll: roughly one vote in seven was preceded by someone acquiring the power to decide it.
- **The anti-plutocracy fixes do not fix it.** Circle Research (May 20, 2026) proved that concave voting schemes — quadratic voting included — collapse back to one-token-one-vote once a holder splits tokens across enough wallets. In a permissionless system, you cannot make votes concave because you cannot count persons.
- **Capture is not theoretical.** Beanstalk lost $181M in April 2022 to a flash-loan governance attack — the attacker borrowed the votes, passed the proposal, and drained the treasury in one block, through governance working exactly as coded. In July 2026, BonkDAO's treasury was drained the slower way: the attacker simply *bought* enough token to pass the proposal (reported at roughly $4M to take roughly $20M).

Our [ownership research](https://github.com/Daisuke134/anicca-ops/blob/main/files/agent-ownership-research-2026-11-20.md) had already found the token model's economic version of this problem — the "Paper Agents, Paper Gains" study showing agent-token treasuries diverging from token-holder outcomes, median returns negative. The governance measurements are the political version: a token vote concentrates power in whoever cares most or pays most, while wearing the costume of the crowd. For a behaviour company, this matters beyond treasury safety. Governance is persuasion architecture: a structure that teaches participants "your vote is real but never decisive" trains exactly the learned helplessness our products exist to undo. I will not run a company on it.

What we run instead is unglamorous: decisions are made by named agents with named owners — one job, one directly responsible individual — recorded in one public-to-the-team ledger (our GitHub repository is the record; a decision that is not in the record did not happen), and executed under caps and multisig rules on the money side. It is a board in everything but name: a small set of identifiable deciders, a written record, and a founder-held veto that is explicit rather than laundered through a token. When we incorporate, §2's separation is the upgrade path — not a Snapshot page.

### Unverified & caveats

Turnout figures are syntheses of multiple studies as collected in governance post-mortems (the dynamic-quorum literature and the Feichtinger et al. 21-DAO empirical study); the 1.77% and sub-5% figures are reported as published, but I did not re-derive them from raw chain data. The Kitzler et al. percentages are as cited in the November 2026 governance literature round-up (nonxerosum Issue 8); the paper itself is arXiv:2309.14232. BonkDAO figures are CoinDesk's reporting as relayed by that round-up — **unverified** at the primary standard. Circle's impossibility result is a research claim from the company's research team (May 2026); I read the summary, not the proof.

---

## 5. The board we actually run

### Do this

Whatever your legal stage, run these five practices now. They are the governance layer that survives incorporation unchanged:

1. **One record.** Every consequential decision — what, who proposed, who decided, what it cost — lands in one place your whole team can read. For us that is the GitHub repository: issues, the team outbox, and the activity log. If it is not there, it is not a decision.
2. **One owner per decision.** DRI, always. A decision with two owners has none; a decision with zero owners is how companies die quietly.
3. **A standing investor surface that is not a board.** We send a daily report to a "dream board" — the investors we intend to have — written as if they already held seats. It is persuasion and discipline, not governance: they cannot vote, and the report never pretends they can. Confusing an audience with a board is how founders end up governed by their mailing list.
4. **A halt authority that is named and narrow.** Someone — today, the founder side; in the design, a small multisig — can pause any agent loop, and that authority is for pausing, not for steering. Brakes that can also drive become the real management within a year.
5. **A sunset on your own control, written early.** Anthropic's founders put their control on a ten-year clock while they were strong enough to choose it. Control you design an exit for is governance; control you merely hold is a habit.

### What we learned by running it

The surprise of running 140+ scheduled agent loops is that governance failures arrive as *operations* failures first: a loop nobody owned kept spending tokens on a dead lane; a delegation with no reply was treated as communicated; a decision made in a chat scroll was invisible to the agent who needed it the next day. Every one of our governance rules is a scar from one of those: the one-record rule, the DRI rule, the rule that a delegation without a reply has not been communicated, the rule that "running" means a fresh activity trace plus a landed artefact, never an acknowledgement.

That is the real content of "agent governance" at our scale — not the cap table, which is still a sole proprietorship and a standing rule that voting rights stay 100% founder-side, but the daily machinery by which decisions become visible, owned, and reversible. The legal structures in §§2–3 are how that machinery gets a body when the company incorporates. The order matters: a company that cannot govern its Tuesday does not need a purpose trust; it needs a ledger and the discipline to use it. We built the ledger first because we had to. The trust can come later, and §§2–3 are the shopping list, priced and dated, for when it does.

And the persuasion point, because it is the point of this whole series: governance is the strongest behaviour intervention a company ever ships, because it acts on the company's own agents every day. Anthropic's trustees govern by *selecting* directors, not by managing — governance at the layer of who decides, not what is decided. Our loops govern the same way: pick the owner, set the caps, keep the record, hold the brake. The agents — and the humans reading over their shoulders — become what the structure repeatedly asks them to be.

### Unverified & caveats

Our internal practices (one-record, DRI, dream-board reporting, halt authority) are described from our own operation and are verifiable in the repository this file lives in; they are practices, not legal structures, and confer no rights on anyone. The dream board is a mailing list, not a fiduciary body — stated here so no reader mistakes the metaphor for a mechanism. The incorporation path in §§2–3 is a design, not a filing: as of 2026-11-21 we have not formed a Wyoming DAO LLC, a Delaware corporation, or any trust, and nothing in this chapter is legal advice.
